A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiffusionGuard study and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original experiments and appendix material can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original InpaintGuardBench experiments, human evaluations, ablations, purification tests, and black-box transfer results in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on instruction-based editing, sampler variations, larger masks, perturbation visibility, and localized editing.

M1.justification: The core early-step objective and contour-based mask augmentation remain unchanged. Appendix J.1 adds an exploratory variant that separately optimizes perturbations for three facial subregions and merges them. Appendix E.4 also applies the early-step objective without mask augmentation to InstructPix2Pix.

E1.justification: The original 42-image benchmark is retained, but evaluation expands beyond background inpainting to mask-free instruction editing, edits inside sensitive regions, and identity replacement within an existing scene. Appendices E.5 and K also introduce explicit tests with enlarged masks and broader mask-size conditions.

E2.justification: PhotoGuard, AdvDM, Mist, and SDS(-) remain the external protection baselines. Retained comparisons preserve their membership, and the additional protection experiments reuse this set. InstructPix2Pix is an additional editing target rather than a new protection baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include DDIM sampling with 25, 40, and 75 steps, DPM-Solver with 25 steps, and two dilated test masks averaging 26% larger than the training mask. Appendix H adds clean-versus-protected image evaluation using PSNR, SSIM, L2, and DreamSim. The newly stated DDIM-50 and post-processing settings for existing experiments are disclosures, not demonstrated protocol changes.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of sampler sensitivity and generalization beyond shrinking masks, a perturbation-visibility analysis, comparisons explaining editing-model failures, localized-edit protection tests, and a sub-perturbation ablation. These substantially extend the original loss, mask-augmentation, resource-budget, purification, and transfer analyses. Figure 14 merely plots resource-budget results already tabulated in v1.

E5.justification: Appendix J.1 newly reports averaging 32 differently seeded generations per prompt for its single-source-image experiment. The existing human-survey aggregation and 95% confidence intervals remain unchanged. This does not establish increased repetitions for the original experiments, and the new averages lack accompanying uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Original numerical results, including Table 1 and the transfer table renumbered from 7 to 10, remain unchanged. v2 adds substantial results in Tables 7–9, 11–12 and new qualitative comparisons. For example, on InstructPix2Pix, DiffusionGuard has lower CDS than PhotoGuard, 14.07 versus 15.02, but worse PSNR, 17.42 versus 17.19. Table 8 has an apparent metric-column mismatch, limiting interpretation of its individual values.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, equations, and formal setup are retained, with no new theorem, proof, or derivation. Changing 'minimizing' to 'maximizing' before Equation 5 aligns that sentence with the existing arg-max expression; the equations themselves are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about the early-step objective, mask augmentation, benchmark, efficiency, robustness, and transferability. The title replaces 'image editing' with 'inpainting', clarifying the existing focus. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine the headline contributions.

C2.justification: New appendices substantially expand explanations of applicability: instruction-based editing can preserve unwanted structures or alter identity; localized protection can survive because perturbations outside the edited region remain inputs; and larger masks constrain backgrounds and clothing. Appendix J also interprets the limited benefit of merged sub-perturbations. The original closed-model and personalization limitations are retained, moving from Appendix H to L.

D1.justification: Appendix D supplies important missing details of the original pipeline: empty-prompt perturbation optimization, DDIM with 50 inference steps, and copying the retained source region onto generated outputs before demonstrations and numerical evaluation, except Figure 2. New appendices specify additional mask construction and prompt procedures. The abstract changes the code-access pointer from a repository to a project page; both versions already claim public code.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds SPM, MACE, and SepME to the concept-erasure discussion, while new experiments introduce references for DreamSim, DDIM, and DPM-Solver. Appendix I further motivates the focus on inpainting relative to InstructPix2Pix. The principal novelty positioning against existing protection methods remains intact.

P1.justification: The main narrative and most existing prose remain unchanged. v2 revises the title and publication header, makes localized wording corrections, expands acknowledgments, and extends the appendix organization and contents. The added scientific sections do not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables and ten figures, including raw-versus-composited outputs, visibility comparisons, editing case studies, and a sub-perturbation workflow. Figure 14 redisplays existing resource-budget data, Figure 7 is reformatted, and retained appendix figures are renumbered or relocated. This substantially expands the visual presentation while preserving the original image examples.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central robustness claims through sampler and enlarged-mask tests, and adds direct perceptual measurements for previously less-developed visibility claims. Disclosing the optimization prompt, sampler, and source-region compositing also resolves important reproducibility ambiguities. The apparent column mismatch in Table 8 and the single-image scope of Appendix J limit parts of the new evidence, but the gains in validation and transparency clearly outweigh these localized weaknesses.
